story.head: The Devils’ power play has a target
paras: The Jets won the teams’ first meeting this season, 4-2 in Winnipeg on Nov 10. Both teams come in on a three-game winning streak. Going in, the Jets are fifth in the Central (tied for ninth in the NHL) and the Devils second in the Metropolitan (fifth).
The Jets’ record (.593) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.524), largely thanks to pulling off wins in one-goal games. The Devils’ record (.692) is about what their chances are worth.

The Devils (3rd lowest) and the Jets (4th lowest) both keep things calm after the whistle. The Jets get their shots through better than almost anyone (3rd). They also create more chances on the penalty kill than almost anyone (2nd), and that sets up a fight with the Devils’ power play (5th), which could do real damage against the Jets’ penalty kill (28th). As for the Devils, they rarely throw hits (2nd lowest) and draw more penalties than they take (3rd). New Jersey has scored 3.73 goals a game, the fourth most in the league. The Devils shoot a lot, but the Jets don’t.

Kyle Connor (22 G / 16 A / 38 P in 27 GP) leads the Jets in scoring and is fifth in the NHL, with twelve points in his last five games and five goals in seven games against New Jersey since 2023-24. Mark Scheifele (9 G / 25 A / 34 P in 27 GP) isn’t far behind, with eight points in his last five games. Jack Hughes (11 G / 23 A / 34 P in 26 GP) leads the Devils in scoring and is tied for seventh in the NHL, with seven points in his last five games.
Stuart Skinner (9-5-4 / .892 SV% in 19 GS) will likely start for Winnipeg, and Connor Hellebuyck (9-1-0 / .900 SV% in 11 GS) for New Jersey.

At home, Sheldon Keefe likes to send Meier, Hughes and Brown out against opponents’ second lines, so watch for them against Iafallo, Lowry and Björck. One more thing: the Devils usually control more of the chances than the Jets do.
